e.t: Aara is a proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:1. The available lexical information preserves Aara as the name itself and does not provide an additional ordinary-language definition or explanation of its meaning. Therefore, it is best understood simply as a personal name whose precise identity and significance depend on the surrounding genealogical context, which is not included here.

This adjective means “unswerving”: staying firm and not turning aside. It describes someone or something characterized by steady direction, commitment, or purpose rather than hesitation or deviation. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense is clear from the lexical definition, while the surrounding verse determines precisely what person, action, or quality is being described in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX adjective means “salty,” describing something that has the taste or character of salt. It is a straightforward word for saltiness rather than a separate title, name, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, in descriptions connected with places and waters. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the same: having salt or being salt-like in taste.

Amada is a personal name, also rendered “Amatha.” It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Genesis 36:26. Because the available text does not include the surrounding verse, its specific role in that genealogy cannot be described here; its lexical function is simply that of a proper name identifying a person.

Amessia is a proper name identifying a person named in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; its function is to distinguish one individual from others. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 6:30. Without the surrounding verse text, the person’s specific role or significance cannot be explained from the name alone. The clearest meaning is therefore the personal name “Amessia.”

This verb means to accept in turn—to receive or take something when one’s turn comes. It describes an action of accepting rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but the central idea remains receiving something successively or in an ordered sequence.

d: pierce through; fix on a spit

e.h: Pierce Through or Fix on a Spit
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to pierce through or to fix something on a spit. It describes a direct physical action involving piercing and securing an object. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:22. Without the verse text and its surrounding context, the precise object and situation cannot be stated, but the word’s basic sense remains the act of piercing through or fastening on a spit.

This noun refers to cooling, refreshing relief—something that brings release and renewed ease. It can describe relief as a welcome refreshment after weariness, heat, or pressure, though the surrounding verse is needed to show its precise force. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Psalms, Jeremiah, and Hosea. Its central idea remains a refreshing change that eases distress or restores comfort.

This Greek LXX verb means “acknowledge in turn.” It describes responding to another acknowledgment with a corresponding recognition. Its basic sense is reciprocal: one person answers by acknowledging what another person has acknowledged. The word occurs six times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Ezra, Psalms, Daniel, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This adjective describes something free from interference and therefore uninterrupted. It points to activity, progress, or conditions that continue without obstruction or disruption. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:28. The word itself gives a general description rather than naming a person or object; the surrounding verse determines what is uninterrupted in that particular setting.

This Greek LXX verb means “die”: to come to the end of one’s physical life. It is an action word used for the event of death, whether describing what happens to a person or stating that someone will die. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs 521 times, so it is a broadly used word for death rather than a term limited to one kind of situation. Its first recorded occurrence is Genesis 2:17. [The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding text.]

This Greek LXX noun means “distancing” or “departure”: moving away from a person, place, position, or allegiance. It describes separation rather than closeness or continued attachment. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including passages in Joshua, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one verse depends on what or whom someone is leaving, but its central idea remains a turning away or moving apart.

This verb means “slung” or “cast.” It describes an action in which something is sent outward rather than simply held or carried. As a verb, it focuses on the act of casting, while the surrounding passage determines what was cast and why. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:21. That single occurrence identifies it as an action word expressing the movement of something being cast or slung, without by itself specifying the object or purpose.

This word means “chief cup-bearer,” a noun identifying the leading person connected with serving the ruler’s cup. It refers to an official position rather than to a general description of drinking or hospitality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs eight times, all in Genesis, especially in the account involving Pharaoh’s servants. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the chief cup-bearer or principal official in that role.

Asōthi, also rendered Asothi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament text, though the available information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 11:29. Its meaning is therefore its identifying name, not a general concept or instruction.

Baithanam is a proper name for a place, also rendered “Vethanam.” It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or person, but a geographic name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once in this corpus, in Joshua 15:59. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise location or significance cannot be explained further here; its basic meaning is the name of that place.

Baria, also rendered Varia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, appearing three times in two verses: twice in Genesis 46:17 and once in Numbers 26:28. The name itself does not provide a general concept or spiritual principle; its meaning is its role as a personal designation. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the individual being named in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX adjective means “hurtful,” describing something that causes harm, pain, or injury. It functions as a describing word rather than naming a person or action by itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Proverbs 10:26. Its basic sense is therefore direct and limited: it identifies something damaging or painful. The precise force of the adjective in that verse depends on the noun or situation it describes, but “hurtful” gives its clear ordinary meaning.

Boukias, also rendered Vukias, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles, at 1 Chronicles 25:4 and 25:13. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or his role. Its precise significance in either reference therefore depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “shower” or “rain,” referring to water falling from the sky. It names ordinary rainfall rather than an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms, and is rendered “rain” in each occurrence. The word’s basic meaning is therefore clear and concrete: a shower of rain or rainfall. Its precise significance in either psalm depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are needed to explain how the image functions there.

This word means “land” or “country,” referring to a stretch of earth or a particular territory. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and may describe a broad region or the land associated with a people. The word occurs seven times in seven Old Testament verses, including passages in 2 Kings, Ezra, Psalms, and Ezekiel. Its exact sense in any verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes the territory itself or the people connected with it.

This word means “mother,” referring to a female parent. It is a noun used to identify the woman who gives birth to or raises a child. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:12, and its rendering there is “mother.” The word’s basic meaning is therefore direct and familiar: it names a child’s mother. The particular emphasis or relationship intended in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself carries this clear family meaning.

Golan is a proper name rendered as “Golan.” In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, at 1 Chronicles 6:56. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, it is best understood here simply as the name Golan rather than assigned an additional meaning or significance. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

This LXX verb means “cease”: to stop or no longer continue. It describes an action, process, or activity coming to an end rather than continuing. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament, across passages from 1 Samuel through Daniel. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is said to have stopped, but its central idea remains cessation—the ending or interruption of something that had been happening.

This verb means to whisper among themselves, describing quiet speech shared privately by a group. It focuses on speaking softly to one another rather than addressing people openly. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 12:18. The wording identifies an action, while the surrounding verse would be needed to determine the exact situation or force of that whispering. Its central idea remains discreet, low-voiced conversation among people.

This noun means “faction”: a divided group formed when people separate from one another rather than act as one. It describes the condition or presence of such division, not a person’s name or an action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 3:29. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This adjective describes something hollow or something that sinks into hollows. It presents a physical shape or condition rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus 13, at Leviticus 13:30 and 13:31. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a hollowed or inward-sinking appearance.

This word means “there,” pointing to a particular place or location. As an adverb, it tells a reader where someone or something is, goes, remains, or acts. It is a common location word in the Greek Old Testament, occurring 734 times across the LXX corpus, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its exact force in any sentence depends on the place or action described nearby.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to “purge” or “clear away”—to remove something unwanted so that it is gone. It can describe clearing land, removing people from among a community, or cleansing away impurity, but its central idea remains decisive removal. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being removed and the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “spread out.” It describes the action of extending something outward rather than keeping it gathered or confined. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, showing a recurring action that can be understood from its immediate sentence and surrounding context. Its basic sense remains focused on outward extension or dispersal, while the precise object being spread depends on the verse in which it occurs.

This noun refers to low, wet ground beside rivers—a marsh or meadow shaped by nearby water. It describes a physical landscape rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 12 times, including passages associated with the Nile, rivers, and land affected by dryness. The central idea remains land that is low and naturally connected with water. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “putting into,” describing the act of placing something inside or introducing it. It is a noun, so it names that action rather than expressing a command to perform it. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:7. The precise significance of the action in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s basic sense remains the act of putting something into something else.

This noun refers to a pledge—something taken or given as security for an obligation. It can describe the act of taking property as a pledge or the pledged item itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Ezekiel 18, where it is rendered “pledge.” Its central idea is a possession connected with a debt or promise, held as security until the obligation is fulfilled. The precise force in each occurrence depends on its surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “bend”: to curve, flex, or cause something to turn from a straight position. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its precise force depends on what is being bent in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 20 times across 19 verses, including passages in Psalms, Jeremiah, and other books. The word’s central idea remains physical or figurative bending, turning, or directing something away from its former line.

This noun refers to scorn or contempt—the attitude of treating someone or something as beneath respect or worth. It names disdain rather than an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 89:5, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains the idea of contempt: a low estimation that dismisses or dishonors its object.

This Greek LXX verb means “send after” or “send upon.” It describes the act of dispatching someone or something onward, either following another person or thing or directing it onto someone or something. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its basic idea is an intentional sending or placing by command. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being sent and where it is directed.

This adverb means “on the surface” or “superficially.” It describes something done or understood only at an outward or shallow level, rather than with depth. In ordinary reading, it can point to an appearance, judgment, or action that does not reach beneath what is immediately visible. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 2:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains a contrast between surface-level treatment and deeper understanding.

This verb means “collect together”: to bring people or things together into one gathering. It describes an action of gathering rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 17:7. The word’s basic sense is therefore focused and specific: things or people are assembled together, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being gathered and for what immediate purpose.

In the Greek Old Testament, this word is identified as “Ereō; Ereo” and functions as a proper name. Its precise reference or role must be understood from the sentence where it appears, since no verse text is available here. It occurs 3,328 times in the Greek LXX corpus, from Genesis through Song of Songs, so it is broadly distributed rather than limited to one passage or book.

This verb means to ennoble someone or to treat and honor them nobly. It describes an action that gives dignity or expresses honorable conduct toward another person, rather than merely identifying a person’s status. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 10:13. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how this honorable treatment functions in that passage.

“Rhythmical” describes something marked by rhythm, regular movement, or an orderly cadence. It is an adjective, so it characterizes a person, action, sound, or thing rather than naming one itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Esther 4:17. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense points to something arranged or proceeding with recognizable rhythm and order.

This noun refers to stability, good health, or vigour—the condition of being sound, strong, and well established. It can describe healthy strength or steady well-being rather than a particular action. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs five times, so its meaning is established but relatively uncommon. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject. The word appears in Esther, Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees.

The word means “Hēth,” functioning as a noun or name rather than describing an action or quality. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at Psalms 118:57. Because the verse text and broader context are unavailable here, its precise role in that occurrence cannot be explained further. It should therefore be understood simply as the name Hēth, without adding another English meaning.

Tharaka is a proper name, referring to a specific named figure rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears twice, once in 2 Kings 19:9 and once in Isaiah 37:9. Those references are parallel accounts, but the available information here does not provide the surrounding verse text or additional details about the person named. The word itself functions as a personal designation: it identifies someone by name.

This noun means “determination”: a firm intention or settled will to do something. It describes purposeful resolve rather than a passing thought or wish. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 13 times, showing that it can describe determined purpose in different settings. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a deliberate decision or strong resolve. The word occurs in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical portions of the LXX corpus.

This word refers to a maid or handmaid—a female servant in a household. As a noun, it identifies the woman serving in that role rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within four Old Testament verses. Its use includes household servants mentioned in Exodus and a handmaid considered in Job, so the central idea is a woman under another household’s authority or service. The exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “noise; bustle,” referring to a noisy disturbance or busy commotion. As a noun, it names the sound or activity itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, in Wisdom 1:10 and 1 Maccabees 9:39. One recorded rendering is “noise,” which fits the central sense. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine whether the word emphasizes loud sound, public commotion, or general disturbance in either passage.

Iasol is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Zechariah 14:5. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain who Iasol is or what role the person has in that passage. Its precise significance there must therefore be understood from the surrounding context of Zechariah 14:5.

This noun means “chariot-road,” referring to a road or course intended for chariots. It names a route associated with the movement or racing of chariots rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, in Genesis and 3 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any particular verse depends on how the surrounding passage uses the road, but its central meaning remains a roadway or course for chariots.

Iseriēl, also rendered Iseril, is a proper name referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 25:14. The name itself identifies the individual, but without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific family connection or role cannot be stated responsibly. Its meaning should therefore be understood as a personal designation within that genealogical or historical record.

This word means “and I.” It is a conjunction that joins the speaker with a preceding person, action, or statement, adding the speaker as another participant or subject. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 85 times across 79 verses, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its basic sense remains straightforward: it connects “I” with what has already been mentioned. The surrounding sentence determines whether the connection adds the speaker to an action, a group, or a continuing thought.

This noun means “evil-doing”: the carrying out of actions that are morally wrong or harmful. It names wrongdoing as an activity rather than describing a person who does it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, it occurs twice—once in Ezra and once in 3 Maccabees. The word’s basic sense remains focused on the practice or act of doing evil; the surrounding passage determines what particular wrongdoing is meant in each occurrence.

This noun means “karasim; sodomites,” referring to people designated by that term. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 35:19. The available lexical meaning identifies the word’s basic reference, while the single occurrence indicates that it is rare within this corpus. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the term functions there.

This Greek LXX verb means to bring someone’s life to an end—that is, to cause a person to die. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in Amos 7:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains clear: ending a person’s life. This is a distinct LXX word and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament lexical entry.

This Greek LXX verb means to cover something with silver. It describes the action of applying silver as a covering or surface treatment, rather than naming the silver itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Exodus 27:17. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of silver-covering.

This noun means “formation of honeycombs”: it names the process by which honeycomb structures come into being, rather than a person, creature, or finished object. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 14:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s particular force in that sentence cannot be described further; its lexical meaning remains focused on the forming of honeycombs. The term is therefore a precise noun for honeycomb formation.

This word means “oven,” referring to a heated place used for baking or cooking. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used twelve times, including descriptions of ovens connected with food preparation and with the effects of intense heat. Its basic sense remains practical and concrete: a structure or appliance in which food is baked. The surrounding passage determines what is being baked or how the oven is being mentioned.

This noun means “power” or “might”—the strength or capacity to accomplish something. It describes effective force rather than merely an inward feeling or intention. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 45:4, and is rendered “might.” Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise role in that verse cannot be described beyond this central meaning. Its normal sense points to strength that enables action or achievement.

This noun means “creature,” referring to a being or thing that has been created. It is a general word rather than a title for one particular kind of creature, so its precise reference depends on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs six times, in Wisdom, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. The English rendering is singular or plural according to its use, but the central meaning remains “creature.”

Latousiim is a proper name, also given as Latusim. It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Genesis 25:3. The name itself does not provide further information about the person’s character, role, or significance; those details must come from the surrounding passage and the wider biblical account.

This word means “lamp stand,” the object designed to hold or support lamps. It is a noun referring to a furnishing rather than to the lamp itself. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, it is used 35 times, especially in descriptions of sacred furnishings and their construction. Its earliest recorded use is in Exodus 25:31, and it continues to appear through 1 Maccabees 4:50. The precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and description.

Maeber (also known as Maever) is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 4:12. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its precise referent must be determined from that passage rather than from the name alone.

“Malchia; Malkhia” is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 9:12. The name itself does not provide enough information to explain the person’s role, family, or significance. Those details would require the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Megediēl, also rendered Meyethil, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Genesis 36:43 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:54. Without the surrounding verse text, no further personal details or significance can be stated from the name alone.

This noun refers to “blame” or “censure”—an expression of finding fault or reproach. It names the criticism directed toward someone rather than an action of forgiving, helping, or judging. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times: three times in Job and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but its central idea remains an accusation or expression of fault-finding.

This verb means “take off,” describing movement away from a place or position. It is an action word: someone or something departs, is removed, or moves away, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, so its basic sense is clear but its exact force still depends on the surrounding words and passage. The word appears in 2 Kings, Psalms, and Proverbs, showing that it can be used in both narrative and wisdom contexts.

This adjective describes something raised up from the ground or hanging above it. It can refer to a physical position, emphasizing elevation rather than something resting on the earth. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 16 times, so its basic sense is used across several passages and settings. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to something suspended, lifted, or positioned above the ground. Its core idea remains simple: elevated, suspended, or hanging rather than grounded.

The word means “mystic,” referring to a person described by that designation. It is a noun, so it names someone rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it appears once, in Wisdom 8:4. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, no more specific contextual force can be stated; the supported lexical meaning is simply “mystic.”

Naarai, also rendered Naare, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:37. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s personal identity and role must be learned from that passage rather than from the name itself. Its basic meaning is therefore a personal designation: Naarai or Naare.

Nisia is a proper name, functioning as the personal designation of someone named Nisia. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, this name occurs once, at Nehemiah 7:56. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, no further identification or contextual detail can be stated from the name alone.

This verb means “make a den”—to create or prepare a sheltered place where something can live. It is a Greek LXX verb found once in the Greek Old Testament, at Isaiah 13:22. Because the word appears only once and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic idea remains straightforward: forming a den or dwelling place rather than merely being present in one.

“Slumber” refers to a state of sleep or drowsiness. As a noun, the word names this condition rather than describing sleeping as an action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Job 33:15. The word presents sleep or drowsiness as a recognizable condition, while the precise force of its use there depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning is simple: slumber, a state of being asleep or very sleepy.

This word means “chamber,” referring to a room or enclosed space within a building. It is a noun, so it names a physical place rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament data provided here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:33. Its basic sense identifies a particular room or chamber; the precise significance of that chamber in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This verb means “pare nails,” describing the act of trimming or cutting nails. It is an action word rather than a name for the nail itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, with most occurrences in Leviticus and Deuteronomy and one later occurrence in 2 Samuel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning remains the practical action of paring or trimming nails.

This Greek LXX verb means “set upright”: to raise something into a standing or properly placed position. It describes an action rather than a person or object, focusing on making something upright. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, across Genesis, Ezra, Esther, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being set upright and the surrounding sentence.

This word is a pronoun meaning “this” or “he,” pointing to a person, thing, or subject already identified in the sentence or surrounding passage. It can identify something near at hand or refer back to someone or something previously mentioned. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs 2,816 times, showing that it is a common word used in many kinds of statements. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding context, but its basic function is to point out or identify.

This Greek LXX verb means “strike”: to hit or deliver a blow. It describes a direct physical action rather than a feeling, opinion, or general kind of trouble. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times across 17 verses, so it is used for this action in several different settings. The surrounding verse determines who strikes, what is struck, and whether the action is carried out by a person or through an event. Its basic meaning remains the act of striking.

This Greek LXX verb means “station”: to place or assign someone in a particular position or location. It describes an act of setting a person where they are intended to stand or serve, rather than merely describing the person’s presence. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is deliberate placement or appointment in a position.

e.h: A Word for By This Time
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “by this time”. It points to a time already reached by the moment under discussion, functioning as a time expression rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Psalms 69:4. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its ordinary contribution is to mark something as occurring or being true by that time.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “poverty” or “need”—a condition of lacking sufficient resources. It describes material want rather than a feeling or an action. The word appears nine times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Proverbs, where it is associated with the consequences of laziness, neglect, or failure to accept correction. It also appears in Job. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains an experience of material lack.

This verb means “stand around” or “stand clear.” It describes people taking a standing position around something or keeping themselves apart from it, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs six times, including passages from Joshua, Samuel, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic idea remains physical positioning: being situated around something or deliberately standing away from it. The surrounding words determine which sense is intended in a particular verse.

This Greek LXX verb means “turn around”: to change direction by turning from one way toward another. It describes an action or movement rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing once in Genesis and twice in Numbers.
